title: The Future of MCP — David Soria Parra, Anthropic

primary.label: Tools, Protocols & Integrations

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's central subject is MCP protocol design, tool calling, and integration of external systems with agents. MCP is a connectivity protocol and platform substrate used by software builders across many verticals. MCP is in widespread production (110M downloads) and the talk focuses on scaling protocol transport and enterprise adoption for 2026. Assumes familiarity with MCP and agent architecture but is a keynote accessible to practicing AI engineers. A conference keynote presentation with live product demonstrations and roadmap discussion. All evidence anchors are grade said_in_transcript from a single source transcript.

summary: David Soria Parra opens by demonstrating an MCP application—an agent that ships its own UI through an MCP server, portable across ChatGPT, VS Code, and Cursor, requiring shared semantics between client and server. He traces MCP's 18-month evolution from a spec document and SDKs to a protocol with remote capabilities, centralized authorization, elicitation, tasks, and experimental MCP applications. MCP has reached 110 million monthly downloads—used by OpenAI's agent SDK, Google's ADK, LangChain, and thousands of frameworks—reaching that volume roughly twice as fast as React. The central thesis is that 2025 was exploration focused on coding agents, while 2026 brings general knowledge-worker agents into production where multi-app connectivity is essential. No single connectivity solution suffices; a stack combining Skills, MCP, and CLI/Computer use should be used together. Two critical client-side improvements are progressive discovery (tool search to defer loading tools into context until needed) and programmatic tool calling (models write scripts in an execution environment to compose tool calls efficiently). Programmatic tool calling can also be done server-side, as demonstrated by the Cloudflare MCP server, which provides an execution environment instead of individual tools, cutting token usage and latency. Soria Parra criticizes one-to-one REST-to-MCP conversion as producing poor results and urges server authors to leverage MCP's rich semantics—applications, skills over MCP, tasks, and elicitation. On the roadmap, core protocol improvements include a stateless transport protocol proposed by Google (targeting June) to make MCP servers scalable like stateless REST servers, improved async task primitives for agent-to-agent communication, and TypeScript SDK v2 and Python SDK v2 based on lessons learned. Strategic enterprise integrations include cross-app access (single login via identity providers like Okta or Google) and automatic server discovery via well-known URLs. Extension mechanisms will enable skills over MCP, letting server authors ship updated domain knowledge without plugin registries. Soria Parra concludes that MCP is in strong shape, that 2026 is about full connectivity, and that the best agents will use every available method—computer use, CLIs, MCP, and skills.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and vision for MCP applications
sections.summary: Soria Parra demonstrates an MCP application—an agent shipping its own UI via an MCP server, portable across clients like ChatGPT and VS Code. The server ships both an app and tools, enabling simultaneous human and model interaction, which requires shared semantics and a protocol between client and server.

sections.title: Looking back at the evolution of the MCP ecosystem
sections.summary: 18 months ago MCP was just a spec document, a few SDKs, local-only with little more than tools. Since then, remote capabilities, centralized authorization, elicitation, tasks, and experimental MCP applications have been added. The community has built servers ranging from toy projects to production SaaS integrations and private enterprise servers.

sections.title: Ecosystem growth and adoption milestones
sections.summary: MCP has reached 110 million monthly downloads, used by OpenAI's agent SDK, Google's ADK, LangChain, and thousands of frameworks. This volume was reached roughly twice as fast as React. Servers range from toy projects to SaaS integrations and numerous enterprise servers.

sections.title: Moving from exploration in 2025 to production in 2026
sections.summary: 2024 was demos, 2025 was coding agents (the ideal scenario—local, verifiable, developer-present), and 2026 brings general knowledge-worker agents needing connectivity across multiple SaaS apps and shared drives. Connectivity is the most important requirement for these production agents.

sections.title: The 2026 connectivity stack: Skills, MCP, and CLI/Computer use
sections.summary: No single connectivity solution suffices. Skills provide domain knowledge in simple files. CLIs excel for local coding agents with sandboxes and pre-trained tools. MCP is the right choice when you need rich semantics, UI, resources, authorization, governance, and experimental features.

sections.title: Improving client harnesses: Progressive Discovery
sections.summary: Current practice dumps all tools into the context window. Progressive discovery uses tool search to defer loading, pulling tools only when the model needs them. Demonstrated with Claude Code showing massive context reduction.

sections.title: Programmatic tool calling and agent orchestration
sections.summary: Instead of sequential tool calls with inference between each, give the model a REPL or execution environment to write code that composes tool calls. MCP's structured output feature provides type information for composition. This enables efficient single-call orchestration and can also compose with CLIs and APIs.

sections.title: Best practices for designing agents and server authors
sections.summary: Soria Parra criticizes one-to-one REST-to-MCP conversion as producing poor results and urges designing servers from a human-interaction perspective. He recommends server-side programmatic tool calling (e.g., Cloudflare MCP server providing an execution environment instead of individual tools) and leveraging MCP's rich semantics—applications, skills over MCP, tasks, and elicitation—that only MCP can offer.

sections.title: Future roadmap for the MCP protocol and core improvements
sections.summary: Core protocol improvements are needed. Current streamable HTTP is hard to scale for hyperscalers; Google has proposed a stateless transport protocol targeting June. The async task primitive (agent-to-agent communication) is experimental and needs broader client support. TypeScript SDK v2 and Python SDK v2 are planned based on lessons learned, with the community-built Fast MCP acknowledged as superior to the current Python SDK.

sections.title: Strategic integrations and enterprise features
sections.summary: Enterprise-focused cross-app access will allow single login via identity providers (Google, Okta) to use MCP servers without re-authentication. Server discovery via well-known URLs will let crawlers, browsers, and agents automatically find MCP servers associated with a website. Both features target the June specification release.

sections.title: Upcoming extension mechanisms and skills over MCP
sections.summary: MCP extension mechanisms will allow differentiated client capabilities (e.g., MCP applications require web-based interfaces). Skills over MCP will let server authors ship updated domain knowledge with large MCP servers, describing how tools are supposed to be used, without relying on plugin registries. Some of this is already experimentally possible via a load-skills tool.

sections.title: Conclusion and call for community feedback
sections.summary: Soria Parra concludes that MCP is in strong shape and 2026 is about full connectivity. The best agents will use every available method—computer use, CLIs, MCP, and skills. He invites community feedback through the newly created foundation, Discord, and open-source channels, and shows a final product feature (model writing graphs) powered by an MCP application.
